html:
A campaign against Buddhism in Tang China under Emperor Wuzong, at its height in 845. The state closed thousands of monasteries and forced hundreds of thousands of monks and nuns back into ordinary life.

Wuzong favoured Daoism, but money mattered too. Monasteries held large tax-free estates, bronze statues and many serfs, while the state was short of funds after the An Lushan Rebellion. By official count some 4,600 monasteries and 40,000 shrines were destroyed, over 260,000 monks and nuns were returned to lay life, and temple lands and slaves were seized. Bronze images were melted down for coins.

Other foreign faiths were hit at the same time: Zoroastrians, Manichaeans and the Church of the East, which had brought Christianity to Tang China.

The campaign stopped when Wuzong died in 846, but Buddhism in China never again had the same wealth and power. Schools that needed few texts or buildings, such as Chan (Zen) and Pure Land, came through best.
sum: A campaign against Buddhism in Tang China under Emperor Wuzong, at its height in 845. The state closed thousands of monasteries and forced hundreds of thousands of monks and nuns back into ordinary life.
